result:
Solution 1 matches the answer I believe is correct, with 1231/420 as the sum; Solutions 2 and 3 do not. I derived most of this but recalled the list of values partly from memory rather than proving it, so confidence is moderate.

**Lower bound of 2/3 for every pair.** Take blue K_{S,T} between two parts S and T. It is H₂-free because H₂ is non-bipartite. Put a red high-girth, high-chromatic graph inside S, and a red complete bipartite graph inside T. Both are H₁-free, since H₁ is 3-chromatic and so contains an odd cycle. Balancing the minimum degrees of S and T gives 2/3 when the red graph inside S has density d = 0. For d = δ_χ(H₁) ∈ {1/3, 1/2}, the balance gives (2−d)/(3−2d), which is 5/7 and 3/4 respectively.

**Upper bound of 4/5.** A graph with minimum degree above 4n/5 contains K₆(t). Since R(3,3) = 6, this forces a monochromatic K₃(t), which contains both H₁ and H₂. So the threshold is at most 4/5.

**Values in between.** The pentagon blow-up, with red C₅ and blue complement C₅, plus a sparse high-chromatic graph in one part, can reach 4/5 for suitable pairs. My attempt to embed K_{2,2,2} into it did not succeed, so I did not confirm that example. The set {2/3, 5/7, 3/4, 4/5} is what I recall from the literature on this problem.

The sum is 2/3 + 5/7 + 3/4 + 4/5 = 1231/420.

**Solution 2** is incoherent. It cites an IMC result, lists a set of values that is inconsistent with the lower bound of 2/3, and ends with an unsupported answer of 2.

**Solution 3** omits both 3/4 and 4/5, so its sum is too small.

VERDICT 1: ACCEPT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
